tldr: When quadrotor motor thrust drops by roughly half, which control allocator performs best depends on the geometric location of the failed motor. Switching methods via a frozen routing policy conditioned on failure location achieved high-rate safe emergency landings.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the implemented emergency landing system. Nominal motor commands and fault information (failed motor index $m$ and remaining effectiveness $\eta$) feed into a fault-geometry-aware supervisor, which routes commands to the selected control allocator before passing them to the simulator's thrust-reduction block.
overview:
Quadrotors have very low actuator redundancy. When even a single motor suffers a loss of effectiveness (LoE), the available control authority (remaining control geometry) becomes heavily distorted, making safe emergency landing difficult. While standard practice relies on applying a single fault-tolerant control or control allocation scheme, previous work has not sufficiently answered whether the best allocation method changes depending on which motor failed, even under the exact same degree of degradation.

This study evaluates this question in a Crazyflie software-in-the-loop (SITL) environment under a severe scenario where one motor's effectiveness drops by roughly half ($\eta = 0.496$). Comparing three methods—bounded weighted least squares (PINV), a candidate-search residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with weights tuned offline via the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)—revealed a clear split: CEM-tuned QP-lite excelled on M1, M3, and M4 failures, while PINV dominated on M2.

Based on these findings, the authors built a frozen policy routing that switches allocators according to the failed motor position. Evaluated across fresh initial seeds, it achieved 117 safe landings out of 120 trials (a 97.5% success rate). Furthermore, the study quantitatively clarifies how plant modeling errors in mass and thrust coefficient shift control boundaries and change the primary failure mode at touchdown (from vertical speed violations to angular rate violations).
contributions: Quantitatively demonstrated that under partial single-motor loss of effectiveness ($\eta=0.496$), the ranking of the best control allocator reverses depending on the geometric location (index) of the failed motor.
Achieved safe landing success rates above 95% across fresh seeds and a randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation using a frozen routing map conditioned on fault geometry.
Precisely identified the critical safe landing boundary ($\eta_{50} \approx 0.4956$) for the highly sensitive M2/PINV condition using Firth logistic regression.

Conducted one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) plant perturbation experiments, clarifying how errors in mass and thrust coefficient affect control limits and shift the primary first-contact violation criterion from vertical speed to angular rate.

sections.heading: Does the best allocator change depending on which motor fails?
sections.summary: This study tests on a Crazyflie simulator whether the best control allocator under partial thrust loss changes depending on the failed motor's location. The problem is tackled across three stages: allocator comparison on development data, validation on fresh seeds with a frozen policy, and sensitivity analysis against plant modeling errors.
sections.details:
Because a quadrotor controls six degrees of freedom with only four motors, it has virtually no redundancy. When one motor experiences a partial loss of effectiveness (LoE), the attainable set of forces and moments (control geometry) is heavily distorted, directly determining whether an emergency landing succeeds or fails.

Typically, control allocation—decoupling high-level motion control from low-level actuator distribution—is used for such problems. Going one step further than standard fault-tolerant control (FTC) studies, this work focuses on a key question: even with the exact same failure severity, does the best allocation algorithm change depending on where the broken motor is located?

Using the CrazySim environment, the authors compare bounded weighted least squares (PINV), a finite-candidate residual search allocator (QP-lite), and a CEM-tuned variant whose parameters were optimized offline via the Cross-Entropy Method. Assuming fault detection is provided externally, the study uses rigorous experimental protocols to isolate how allocator selection depends on fault location and how plant-model mismatch affects that choice.

sections.heading: The evolution of fault-tolerant control and control allocation
sections.summary: Multi-rotor fault-tolerant control has a long history, from attitude recovery under complete rotor loss to adaptive control under partial faults. This study stands out by fixing the fault class and comprehensively investigating the synergy between failed-motor location and allocation algorithms in simulation.
sections.details:
### II-A Fault-Tolerant Quadrotor Control
For the extreme scenario of complete single-rotor loss, extensive research has explored reduced-attitude control—sacrificing yaw control to maintain attitude while spinning rapidly—as well as nonlinear MPC and upset recovery. For partial thrust loss and model uncertainty, FTC strategies using sliding mode control and adaptive observers have also been proposed. While these prior works show how remaining control authority can be preserved, this paper fixes the fault class and takes a controlled, comparative approach to assess how different allocators perform across each motor location.

### II-B Control Allocation and Simulation
In control allocation, pseudo-inverse (PINV) methods, bounded weighted least squares (WLS), and active-set algorithms are well known. This study uses CrazySim, which runs genuine Crazyflie firmware in SITL paired with Gazebo physics. To accurately capture the boundary between safe and unsafe outcomes in critical regimes, the statistical analysis employs Firth bias-reduced logistic regression, which handles separated data effectively, while parameter tuning is performed offline via the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM).

sections.heading: Fault modeling and strict criteria for a 'safe' touchdown
sections.summary: The authors formalize a single-motor thrust reduction model where one motor command drops by a factor of $\eta$, and establish five strict criteria for first contact. Development trials determine the optimal allocator routing map for each motor index, which is then frozen for evaluation.
sections.details:
### III-A Fault and Safety Model
Let the nominal motor command vector be $\mathbf{u} = [u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4]^\top$. For a damaged motor $m$, the effective command becomes $u_m^{\mathrm{eff}} = \eta u_m$, while healthy motors remain $u_j^{\mathrm{eff}} = u_j$. Here $\eta=1$ represents nominal operation, with smaller values indicating more severe damage. The primary benchmark experiments set an edge-of-envelope condition at $\eta = 0.496$ (an approximate 50.4% thrust reduction).

Each trial is evaluated at the moment of 'first contact', defined as when the quadrotor altitude first reaches $z \le 0.03\,\mathrm{m}$ after fault injection. To be classified as safe, all five strict criteria must be satisfied simultaneously:
- Vertical descent speed: $|v_z| \le 0.35\,\mathrm{m/s}$
- Horizontal speed: $v_{xy} \le 0.25\,\mathrm{m/s}$
- Tilt angle (roll/pitch): $\theta_{rp} \le 12^\circ$
- Angular rate norm: $\|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| \le 1.5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$
- Horizontal drift: $d_{xy} \le 0.75\,\mathrm{m}$
Violating even one criterion marks the trial as unsafe.

### III-B Objective
From development trials, the routing map $g: m \mapsto \pi_m$ assigns each fault index $m$ to an allocator $\pi_m \in \{\pi_{\mathrm{PINV}}, \pi_{\mathrm{QP}}, \pi_{\mathrm{CEM}}\}$. Once established, this policy is completely frozen and evaluated on fresh seeds. Additionally, the critical M2/PINV pairing is thoroughly analyzed for robustness against plant perturbations.

captions.F1: Block diagram of the emergency landing control. The failed motor index $m$ and remaining effectiveness $\eta$ are passed to the supervisor, which selects an allocator according to the predetermined routing map.

sections.heading: Three allocators: bounded WLS, candidate-search QP, and CEM tuning
sections.summary: This section details the three evaluated methods: bounded WLS (PINV), which exhaustively searches 81 active sets in Crazyflie PWM command space; QP-lite, which evaluates candidate residual patterns via surrogate metrics; and a CEM-tuned variant whose scoring weights were optimized offline.
sections.details:
### IV-A Bounded WLS / PINV
This weighted least squares method operates directly in the Crazyflie PWM command space. It minimizes a quadratic cost combining regularization with tracking error against target commands scaled by the fault matrix $D_m(\eta)$. To enforce actuator saturation limits rigorously within the firmware, it performs an exhaustive search across all $3^4 = 81$ active sets (lower bound, free, upper bound) to select the feasible solution with minimum cost. Although labeled 'PINV' following internal project naming, it is not naive clipped pseudo-inverse, but strict bounded WLS.

### IV-B QP-Lite and Offline CEM Tuning
QP-lite applies discrete residuals to the nominal command ($\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_0 + \mathbf{r}$, with $r_m=0$ for the failed motor). It maintains a library of 7 to 8 residual candidates per motor. At the moment of fault detection, it computes surrogate indicators for vertical velocity, horizontal displacement, and tilt, evaluating them in a quadratic scoring function. Rather than solving a continuous quadratic program online, it is a lightweight algorithm that picks the best candidate from a finite set.

For the CEM-tuned variant, the 13 weight parameters in QP-lite's scoring function were optimized offline using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). Tuning utilized near-hover simulator surrogates over $\eta \in [0.4960, 0.4980]$ across all motors, and the resulting parameters were frozen in a JSON file.

### IV-C Frozen Supervisor
Based on development trials, the routing map was frozen to assign the CEM-tuned allocator to M1, M3, and M4 failures, and PINV to M2: $g(1)=g(3)=g(4)=\pi_{\mathrm{CEM}},\ g(2)=\pi_{\mathrm{PINV}}$. This mapping remained fixed throughout all subsequent tests.

sections.heading: Over 3,500 simulation trials and rigorous statistical validation
sections.summary: Using CrazySim (Gazebo Sim 7.9 + ROS 2), 3,570 total runs were executed under a deterministic protocol randomizing initial positions and fault injection times via seeds. Development and validation sets were strictly separated, and statistical significance was evaluated using Firth logistic regression and McNemar tests.
sections.details:
### V-A Environment and Protocol
Experiments ran on CrazySim SITL under Ubuntu 22.04, ROS 2 Humble, Gazebo Sim 7.9, and Python 3.10. The protocol varied initial positions $x_0, y_0 \sim \mathcal{U}(-0.03, 0.03)\,\mathrm{m}$, hover altitude $0.70 \pm 0.02\,\mathrm{m}$, and fault injection time $10.0 \pm 0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ deterministically via random seeds. Across the core evaluation sets alone, 3,570 simulation trials were conducted.

### V-B Development, Validation, and Boundary Estimation
First, 30 seeds per motor (360 trials total) at $\eta = 0.496$ were used to select allocators (development data). The policy was then frozen and verified on a 120-trial holdout test with fresh seeds, as well as a 120-trial integrated-supervisor evaluation in randomized execution order.
For the M2/PINV condition, $\eta$ was varied from 0.49520 to 0.49580 in steps of $10^{-4}$ to estimate the critical 50% success threshold $\eta_{50}$ via Firth bias-reduced logistic regression.

### V-C Plant Sensitivity and Routing Stability
A one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) sensitivity analysis perturbed five plant parameters by $\pm 10\%$ across 10 conditions (2,100 trials total): mass, thrust coefficient, motor time constant, thrust-to-torque ratio, and arm length. For each unsafe landing, violated criteria were counted non-exclusively. McNemar tests were also used to check whether PINV's advantage over CEM on M2 reversed under plant perturbations at $\eta=0.496$.

sections.heading: Allocator specialization by motor index and failure mode shifts under plant error
sections.summary: In development trials, PINV dominated on M2 while CEM led on the other motors. The frozen policy achieved a 97.5% safe landing rate on fresh seeds. Perturbations in mass and thrust coefficient shifted $\eta_{50}$ substantially and switched the primary cause of failure from vertical speed to angular rate.
sections.details:
### VI-A Allocator Complementarity and Frozen Validation
At $\eta = 0.496$, safe landing counts across the 30 development trials for PINV / QP-lite / CEM were:
- M1 failure: 26 / 4 / **30**
- M2 failure: **30** / 6 / 3
- M3 failure: 19 / 28 / **29**
- M4 failure: 0 / 5 / **23**
No single allocator was best across all motors: PINV beat CEM 30 to 3 on M2, whereas CEM was markedly superior on M1 and M4 (and edged ahead 29 to 28 on M3). Freezing this policy and evaluating it on fresh seeds yielded 117/120 safe touchdowns (97.5%) in holdout tests and 115/120 (95.8%) in the integrated-supervisor evaluation.

### VI-B Critical Boundary for Nominal M2/PINV
Varying $\eta$ for the sensitive M2/PINV branch caused safe landings to climb sharply from 0 (at 0.4952) to 30 (at 0.4958). Firth regression estimated the critical threshold $\eta_{50}$ at approximately 0.4956 (within-model 95% bootstrap interval $[0.4955, 0.4956]$), highlighting an extremely steep success-to-failure boundary in simulation.

### VI-C Plant Sensitivity and Criterion Shifts
Under $\pm 10\%$ parameter variations, the thrust coefficient (up to 0.05495 shift) and mass (up to 0.04974 shift) altered $\eta_{50}$ dramatically. This impact was more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of time constant or arm length variations (up to 0.000404).
Equally striking was the shift in violation types. As shown in Figure 6, excessive vertical speed was the primary failure mode in most conditions. However, under mass $-10\%$, vertical speed violations dropped to zero; instead, angular rate was violated 150 times and horizontal speed 72 times. Similarly, thrust coefficient $+10\%$ produced only angular rate violations (22 times). This demonstrates that plant mismatch fundamentally alters the physical breakdown mechanism during landing.

### VI-D Routing Stability at Fixed $\eta$
Testing M2 directly between PINV and frozen CEM at $\eta = 0.496$ across nominal and 10 perturbed plant states showed that PINV achieved a higher safe count in 9 of 11 states, tying in the remaining 2 (both 0/30). Within the range of single-parameter variations tested, PINV's superiority on M2 was never reversed by CEM.

captions.F6: Heatmap of safety criteria violations (non-exclusive counts) at first contact across 10 OFAT plant perturbation conditions. Vertical speed violations dominate most conditions, but the primary cause shifts entirely to angular rate under mass $-10\%$ and thrust coefficient $+10\%$.

sections.heading: Boundaries and open challenges for simulation-based findings
sections.summary: While this study clearly shows allocator complementarity conditioned on fault geometry, the authors acknowledge key limitations, including the lack of real-world flight tests, assuming known fault parameters without an online estimator, and testing single-parameter variations in isolation.
sections.details:
The core contribution of this work is rigorously demonstrating allocator complementarity based on failure geometry under partial motor thrust loss. However, the paper explicitly outlines several limitations and assumptions:

- **No Physical Flight Tests and Known Fault Assumptions**: All experiments were conducted in CrazySim simulation. The failed motor index and degradation ratio $\eta$ were assumed to be known inputs. Online fault detection and identification (FDI), along with estimation latency, were not modeled.
- **Simplified Allocation Models**: Bounded WLS operates on linear relationships in PWM space rather than physical wrench space. QP-lite is an empirical search across finite candidates without global optimality guarantees or mathematical safety proofs like Control Barrier Functions.
- **Limits of OFAT Sensitivity Analysis**: The sensitivity analysis varied only one factor at a time, leaving compound parameter mismatches—such as simultaneous mass and thrust coefficient errors—unexplored.
- **Nature of Touchdown Criteria**: Recorded violation counts reflect the physical failure modes observed at the instant of touchdown, distinct from the active sets (constraint activations) inside the optimization algorithms.

sections.heading: Takeaway: the value of geometry-aware allocation and plant sensitivity checks
sections.summary: The paper concludes that choosing control allocators based on the failed motor's location is highly effective during emergency quadrotor landings. At the same time, because errors in mass and thrust coefficient heavily shift landing limits and failure modes, thorough sensitivity analysis is essential.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that when a quadrotor loses roughly half of one motor's effectiveness, the optimal control allocator depends on the geometric location of the damaged motor. By establishing a frozen routing map from development trials—assigning CEM-tuned QP-lite to M1, M3, and M4, and bounded WLS (PINV) to M2—the system attained a 97.5% safe touchdown rate on fresh seeds.

Sensitivity analysis further uncovered a sharp threshold ($\eta_{50} \approx 0.4956$) in the nominal model, while showing that $\pm 10\%$ mismatches in mass or thrust coefficient shift this threshold by two orders of magnitude more than structural parameters, changing the primary touchdown failure mode from hard vertical impacts to uncontrolled rotation. The work underscores that designing emergency allocation policies requires both matching the allocator to the fault geometry and thoroughly validating sensitivity to plant-model errors.

takeaways: Which control allocation method performs best (bounded WLS vs. candidate search) depends clearly on the geometric location of the failed motor.
Modeling errors in vehicle mass and thrust coefficient ($\pm 10\%$) shift the safe landing threshold by over two orders of magnitude compared to motor time constants or arm lengths.
Plant modeling mismatch can fundamentally alter the primary emergency landing failure mode, shifting it from hard vertical descent to uncontrolled angular rotation.
limitations: All results are based on CrazySim simulations; physical aerodynamic interference, battery voltage sag, and contact impact dynamics remain unvalidated on real hardware.
The failed motor index and effectiveness ratio $\eta$ are assumed to be known, omitting online fault detection and identification (FDI) latencies and misclassifications.
Sensitivity analysis is restricted to one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) perturbations, leaving the coupled effects of simultaneous multi-parameter variations unaddressed.
